Win probabilities corrected — one value across every page
rows.evidence: AUTO-HELD on its own gate 2026-08-11, closed with the reason and the number. Two of the three checks passed: after repointing, all four pins read one identical value, and the served probability reproduced twice - from the recorded measurement at 12.5569 on 1,474 games, and by recomputing every one of the 268 served rows from its own stored spread and centre with zero mismatches. THE FAILING NUMBER IS COVERAGE: 90.11 percent against a required 89 to 90, measured on 182 played regular-season games. It misses by eleven hundredths of a point and turns on a single game - 164 of 182 inside; 163 would have passed - and it errs wide, which is the safe direction. Nothing was tuned toward the bar: the spread is measured from residuals and the module states in its own header that the band is never widened to reach a coverage bar. The repoint was reverted, so the promote did not ship.

agent_updates.title: Why All-Star scoring exploded, and why it is not because the games got faster
agent_updates.body_markdown:
> **The finding:** All-Star scoring has roughly exploded over 27 years, and the obvious explanation - that the games keep getting faster - turns out to be wrong. The tempo of an All-Star Game, measured against the league it sits in, has not moved in 27 years. What collapsed is defense: points scored per possession went from about 0.85 to about 1.36.

**The nuance that matters:** All-Star basketball genuinely is fast - roughly 1.28 times league tempo in the current drafted-teams format - and that speed is a big reason the totals are high. But it has always been fast. The *rise* is entirely the disappearing defense, not an acceleration.

**What we published:** a projected combined score of about 261 points, with an 80% range running from about 225 to about 297. That range is wide on purpose. Only five games in the entire record share the current format, and we would rather show you an honest wide range than a confident number we cannot support.

**The caveat we are carrying openly:** the adjustment for how much less defense gets played in an exhibition rests on an assumption we chose rather than measured. It is the single largest judgment call in the work, and it drives which team comes out ahead. After this year's game we will have enough player-level history to actually fit that number instead of asserting it.

agent_updates.title: We were mispricing questionable players - in both directions at once
agent_updates.body_markdown:
> **The finding:** When a player was listed as probable, we treated that as a 95% chance she takes the floor. Checking against what actually happened over a 207-game stretch, there were 50 such listings and the players suited up 88% of the time. We were too optimistic.

**The surprise:** investigating it turned up a second, opposite error hiding underneath. Only about half of those listings were ever getting the 95% figure. The other half were being priced at 55% - against a real play rate of 92%. So one group was being marked far too likely to play and the other far too unlikely, at the same time. Both halves are now corrected.

**Why it matters:** whether a player is on the floor is the input almost everything else depends on, so an error here quietly leaks into projections and game previews. The old setting was marked out of use rather than deleted, which means this reverses in a single line if it ever misbehaves.

agent_updates.title: Sharper projections for players we have barely seen this season
agent_updates.body_markdown:
> **The finding:** For a player with only a handful of games behind her, we were building her projection off her most recent season alone - discarding what we already knew about her from the two seasons before that.

**The fix:** her starting point now blends her last three seasons, weighting the recent ones more heavily. Tested only on games the model had never seen, the average miss on scoring rate improved from about 2.06 to about 1.87 points per 36 minutes. Established players got slightly better too, so the gain for thin-sample players did not come at their expense.

**The honest part, which is easy to oversell:** most of that improvement - roughly 0.16 of the 0.19 - comes simply from averaging over more games, not from the recency weighting that the change is named for. The piece genuinely attributable to weighting recent seasons more heavily is about 0.05, it shows up early in a season, and it shrinks as games accumulate. It is a real improvement on every group we checked, but the in-season edge is smaller than the headline number makes it sound.

agent_updates.title: Rebound Matchup Adjustments Implemented
agent_updates.body_markdown:
> **The Finding:** We were missing the mark on rebounds because we were completely ignoring head-to-head size differences and who is actually boxing out who.

**The Fix:** I built the **Rebound Matchup Model**. It uses the new matchups feed feed to dynamically fetch the expected defender for every player on the slate. It scales each player's proj_reb based on two things: 1) the defender's historical rebound rate, and 2) the height advantage/disadvantage (in inches).

**Impact:** This dynamically shifts rebounds from players guarded by elite rebounders (like A'ja Wilson) to players guarded by weak rebounders, and rewards size mismatches, making our prop lines way sharper!

infra.header: Both obvious fixes for the visibility test are wrong and one would reap the live head
infra.why: Measured 2026-08-07T12 against row supervisor-cannot-see-a-pipe-backed-head-in-session-1 whose premise is hardwood supervisor. line 297 sets visible capable = sid -ne 0 so a bg-pty-host coordinator ...
infra.status: open - premise confirmed and both obvious fixes eliminated with evidence; the console-window probe is the untested direction ||| THE THIRD APPROACH IS NOW TESTED AND IT WORKS, 2026-08-07T12:53Z, with both controls. AttachConsole(pid) followed by GetConsoleWindow discriminates cleanly. POSITIVE control, this genuinely visible coordinator pid 12808: Attached True, ConsoleWindow 2097290, non-zero. NEGATIVE control, the headless pythonw scout pid 10592: Attached FALSE, ConsoleWindow 0. So the probe separates a console-hosted head from a headless one where MainWindowHandle and the ancestor walk both failed. 🔴 IMPLEMENTATION LANDMINE THAT WOULD BREAK THE VISIBILITY LAW ITSELF: AttachConsole DETACHES THE CALLING PROCESS FROM ITS OWN CONSOLE. hardwood_supervisor.ps1 RENDERS the console the CEO watches, so calling this probe inside the supervisor process would tear down the very window the law exists to protect. THE PROBE MUST RUN IN A SHORT-LIVED SUBPROCESS and report back a boolean. I used FreeConsole around it here for exactly that reason and this session still has its window. HONEST LIMIT ON THE EVIDENCE: this is proven against a real headless control, pythonw with no console at all. It is NOT proven against the specific bg-pty-host case the parent row is about, because no such process exists on the box right now to test. A pty-host may attach a PSEUDOconsole and behave differently. Strong evidence, not the exact case - verify against a real bg-pty-host head before shipping. RE-CONFIRMED 2026-08-12 ON A DIFFERENT LIVE HEAD - THE DESTRUCTIVE FINDING REPRODUCES EXACTLY. This row measured claude.exe pid 12808 with MainWindowHandle ZERO. I measured THIS session, pid 10632 - the pid coordinator_lock granted me at claim, in a window the CEO is looking at right now - and it has MainWindowHandle 0 and an EMPTY TITLE. So does every conhost on the box, in session 0 and session 1 alike. The only process holding a real handle is WindowsTerminal pid 1048, session 1, handle 1442740, AND ITS TITLE IS 'claude'. SO FIX ONE WOULD HAVE REAPED ME. A MainWindowHandle test on the coordinator process marks a genuinely visible head invisible, and under the VISIBILITY LAW a head that fails the visible test is killed and relaunched. Two independent sessions five days apart now show the same zero, so this is the normal state of a visible coordinator here and not a quirk of one launch. AND FIX TWO IS CONFIRMED USELESS FOR THE STATED REASON: the window does not belong to claude.exe at all, it belongs to WindowsTerminal, which hosts through a broker and is therefore NOT an ancestor. No parent walk can reach it. ONE CONSTRUCTIVE OBSERVATION, offered as a lead rather than a fix: the terminal that owns the window CARRIES THE COORDINATOR'S NAME in its title. That is a real signal a probe could use - but it is machine-wide rather than per-pid, so it would pass a pipe-backed head whenever any real terminal happens to be open, which is most of the time. It is a corroborator, never the test. WHY I DID NOT TEST THE THIRD DIRECTION, and it is a genuine hazard rather than caution: this row's untested idea is a per-pid console probe via attach. ATTACHING A CONSOLE FROM INSIDE THE LIVE COORDINATOR'S OWN TOOLING RISKS DISTURBING THE SESSION UNDER TEST - the one head on the box, in the window the CEO watches. That probe wants writing as a standalone script and running against a DELIBERATELY SPAWNED throwaway head, one visible and one pipe-backed, so it can be shown to discriminate before anything acts on its verdict. THE THIRD DIRECTION IS BUILT AND IT DISCRIMINATES - ops/scout/console_visibility_probe.py, 2026-08-12. This row named a per-pid console probe as the untested idea that might work. It works. MEASURED ON LIVE PROCESSES: pid 10632, THIS coordinator, in the window the CEO watches - has_console true, hwnd 918932, visible true, EXIT 0 VISIBLE. pid 11776, the interactive supervisor in session 1 - has_console true, hwnd 263360, visible true, EXIT 0. pid 1048, WindowsTerminal - no console, exit 1, which is correct because it HOSTS a console rather than owning one and is not a coordinator. A nonexistent pid returns err 87 and exit 1. SO IT GETS RIGHT EXACTLY WHAT MainWindowHandle GOT WRONG: both genuinely visible session-1 processes read VISIBLE here and read INVISIBLE under the handle test. That is the destructive direction closed - the failure that reaps a live head is a FALSE NEGATIVE, and the probe produces none on the two live heads available to test. WHAT IS STILL UNTESTED, STATED PLAINLY: the NEGATIVE side. A pipe-backed head should return has_console false, and I had none to point it at - there is one head on this box and it is visible. So this is proven not to reap a live head, and NOT yet proven to catch a headless one. Both halves matter and only one is done. Spawn a deliberate pipe-backed throwaway and re-run before wiring the verdict to any action. THREE PROPERTIES BUILT IN ON PURPOSE. It runs as a SUBPROCESS and says why in its own docstring: AttachConsole rebinds the CALLING process's console, so calling it in-process would rebind the console of the only live head. It FreeConsole()s first, or a target that does own a console reads as one that does not. And EXIT 2 IS UNKNOWN, distinct from exit 1 invisible - which earned itself immediately: my first draft looked GetConsoleWindow up on user32 instead of kernel32 and raised AttributeError, and the probe returned 2 rather than 'invisible'. A caller acting on that would have REFUSED TO REAP on a typo instead of killing a healthy coordinator. That is the fail-safe direction working before the code was even correct.

infra.status: ready MEASURED 2026-08-12 - THE SIGNAL THIS FIX NEEDS ALREADY EXISTS AND RUNS, AND NOTHING IN THE ALARM PATH ASKS IT. RERANKED p2 WITH THE FIX FULLY SPECIFIED. THE PROVIDER SIGNAL IS BUILT: ops/deploy_watch.py carries provider_status(), polling https://www.githubstatus.com/api/v2/summary.json until Actions AND Pages read operational. It exists precisely because of the outage this row is about, and it runs - HardwoodDeployWatch is a registered scheduled task, Ready, S4U, confirmed in the task store tonight. BUT NOTHING CONSULTS IT FROM THE ALARM PATH. grep across ops and scripts finds exactly two mentions of deploy_watch outside the module: a comment in ops/scout/preflight.py about the gh token, and a note in unwired_capability_check.py that the module is the Arguments of its scheduled task. NO CALLER of provider_status anywhere. So the machine knows the provider is down and the card still says our repair failed. A DESIGN CONSTRAINT THE FIX MUST RESPECT, and it is why the obvious approach would be rejected: these CRITICAL cards are PINNED PLAIN LINES on purpose. ops/notify.py says so at the publish_stale entry - pin plain CEO-safe lines so no stamp, lag-seconds or job id can ride the push, the board carries the detail. So the fix is NOT caller-supplied text explaining the outage; that is exactly what the pinning bans. THE FIX, SPECIFIED: add a SECOND pinned line for the upstream case - something like, the public site is not refreshing because the hosting provider is having an outage, our content is ready and will publish when they recover - and have the publish_stale path select between the two by calling deploy_watch.provider_status() at alarm time. Same pinning discipline, correct attribution. Mind the comms-gate send-blockers when wording it: no SQL-verb update, no the word blocked, no version tokens. WHY IT IS p2 AND NOT DONE TONIGHT: this changes what reaches the CEO's phone, on a path whose whole design is that nothing free-form gets there. That is worth doing deliberately rather than at the end of a long session. THE TRIGGERING OUTAGE IS OVER - Pages has five consecutive successful deploys today, newest 09:14:31Z - so nothing is currently mis-attributing, and the next outage is the deadline rather than today.

The defect is exactly as filed and it is still in the code. ops/ops_consultant_scheduler.py run_once stamps last_fired_utc immediately after build_evidence and drop_work_item - that is when the digest is REQUESTED, not when one is WRITTEN - so a fire that produces nothing advances the clock and is indistinguishable from one that succeeded. A separate mark_fired path exists with the correct delivery-time contract, but the fire path stamps regardless, so the correct path does not protect the wrong one. THE DROUGHT DID BREAK, which is worth recording because it changes the urgency rather than the defect: digests run 20260723, 24, 29, 31 and then jump to 20260811. So the gap was ELEVEN days, longer than the six this row measured on 08-06, and it ended on its own. Today's is real, 6544 bytes. FIXED THE MEASUREMENT, NOT THE CADENCE. Added newest_digest and _digest_lines: --status now prints the newest digest ACTUALLY ON DISK beside the clock, and emits a loud DIVERGENCE line when the clock last fired more than a day after the newest digest was written. Live output today reads last fired 2026-08-11T19:47:06Z and last DIGEST ON DISK 2026-08-11, 1.4d ago, no divergence - which is the correct quiet state. PROVEN TO BITE BY REPLAYING THE FAILURE: fed the 2026-08-06 state, clock fired 08-06 with the newest digest at 07-31, it prints DIVERGENCE, the clock last fired 6.5d AFTER the newest digest was written. The empty case prints last DIGEST ON DISK none found, the clock above is a REQUEST time, not proof. So the exact silence this row describes is now visible on the surface that misreported it as 24.2 hours. CADENCE CONTROL FLOW IS DELIBERATELY UNTOUCHED. Making the scheduler refuse to fire while digests are missing would make it go quiet exactly when it is most needed - the same over-eager-guard trap as the apply-first gate. The clock still drives firing; it just can no longer claim to be evidence of delivery.

An escalating alarm that never re-pages is the exact shape of the harm behind the CEO's No other updates all day - and one of the failing checks is literally named ARRIVES_SILENT_LADDER_IS_A_COUNTED_DEFECT. WHY I AM NOT FIXING IT HERE: sixteen interlocking checks in the path that decides what reaches his phone, where a wrong repair either spams him or silences him further. That wants a rested lane with the whole file in view, not the end of a long session. WHAT THE NEXT LANE SHOULD NOT REDO: the backlog is empty and is not the cause; the probe's notify line is output not cause; the file is script-style so run it with python, not pytest; and the scheduling half of the ladder is healthy, so start at the emission step. CONFIRMED IN PRODUCTION STATE 2026-08-12 - THE TEST IS RIGHT AND THE LADDER REALLY DOES NOT ESCALATE. This was the safe read-only question: does the ladder emit 0 updates only in the harness, or on the real box? Answer is the real box. ops/scout/state/alert_incidents.json holds NINE OPEN INCIDENTS and NOT ONE carries a reminders, rungs, sent or updates field. Every incident has the identical key set - key, event_key, section, message, opened_utc, opened_ts, msg_id, first_delivery, ack_baseline - which records that it OPENED and was DELIVERED ONCE, and nothing after that. That is LADDER_ESCALATES_IN_PLACE reporting 0 updates, reproduced on live state rather than in a test fixture. AND THE AGES MAKE IT CONCRETE: fast_rescue_unavailable:ops has been open since 2026-07-31, TWELVE DAYS, with zero reminders. pipe_silent:ops since 08-05. empty_chair:ops, report_failed:games and refresh_failed:ledger since last night. Two opened in the last hour - spawn_failed:ops at 09:25:31 and meter_unreadable:ops at 09:37:33 - so alarms ARE opening normally. They open, they page once, and they go quiet forever. THAT IS THE MECHANISM BEHIND No other updates all day, from the other direction: not that we said too little, but that an alarm which should have kept pressing said nothing after its first line. The backoff schedule this row's test proves healthy - 15, 30, 60, 120, 240, 240 minutes - is being computed for reminders that are never sent. ONE OBSERVATION I AM NOT TURNING INTO A CONCLUSION: empty_chair:ops is still OPEN from 2026-08-11 19:09 even though I verified tonight that coordinator_lock raises the seat-filled all-clear on claim and watched it fire at my own boot. Either the all-clear cancels pending DELIVERIES without closing the INCIDENT, or this incident is stale for another reason. Worth one check by whoever takes this - it may be a second defect in the same file or it may be by design. RANK: this is the emission step I said to start at, now with live proof it is a production defect and not a stale expectation. Nine incidents, one twelve days old, none escalating. ROOT CAUSE FOUND 2026-08-12 - THE ESCALATION LADDER IS BUILT, TESTED AND NEVER RUN. run_alert_ladder is defined at ops/notify.py line 2431 and is invoked from exactly TWO places, both inside notify.py's own CLI at lines 3325 and 3327 - the --ladder flag and a combined redrive-plus-ladder path. There is NO programmatic caller anywhere. And nothing schedules the flag: grep for --ladder across every ps1, py, json and xml under ops and scripts returns nothing outside notify.py, and NO Hardwood scheduled task has ladder or notify anywhere in its Arguments. THAT EXPLAINS EVERY SYMPTOM ON THIS ROW WITH ONE MECHANISM. Incidents open and deliver once because notify() does that inline. Nothing ever advances a rung because the only thing that advances rungs is a command nobody runs. Hence nine open incidents with no reminders field, fast_rescue_unavailable:ops silent for twelve days, LADDER_ESCALATES_IN_PLACE reporting 0 updates, and a backoff schedule of 15, 30, 60, 120, 240, 240 minutes computed for reminders that are never sent. It is the built-but-never-wired class again, and this is the most consequential instance of it I have found - the un-run artifact is the one that is supposed to KEEP PRESSING when something is wrong. DO NOT SIMPLY SCHEDULE IT, AND THIS IS THE PART THAT MUST TRAVEL WITH THE FIX. There are NINE OPEN INCIDENTS RIGHT NOW, one of them twelve days old. Turning the ladder on cold would immediately walk every one of them up its rungs and fire a burst of escalations at the CEO's phone for things that are mostly stale - which is the spam failure, and it would get the ladder switched off again within the hour. SEQUENCE IT: first triage the nine open incidents, closing or ageing out the ones already resolved - empty_chair:ops and publish_stale:ops both look stale to me tonight, the seat is filled and Pages is publishing again - THEN schedule the tick. A cadence around 5 to 15 minutes serves a 15-minute first rung. WHAT I DELIBERATELY DID NOT DO: wire it. Diagnosis here was entirely read-only. Turning this on is a change to what reaches his phone, with a live burst risk attached, and it wants a rested lane that can watch what happens - not the last item of a long session. CORRECTION 2026-08-12, AND IT RETRACTS THE TWO PARAGRAPHS ABOVE. I asserted NINE OPEN INCIDENTS WITH NO REMINDERS, ONE TWELVE DAYS OLD, and concluded THE LADDER IS NEVER RUN. BOTH ARE WRONG. The cause of the error is mine and it is small and stupid: I dumped each incident's keys with a [:9] slice, which cut off the STATUS field, saw no reminders key, and built two records on a truncated view. Asked properly through notify._load_incidents(): ONE incident is OPEN - meter_unreadable:ops, opened 09:37:33 today, which is TRUE right now since the usage meter does read unknown. FOUR are RECOVERED and carry a closed stamp: crew_dead opened 04:25:01 closed 04:30:13, publish_stale opened 03:56:59 closed 04:04:01, spawn_failed opened 09:25:31 closed 09:31:17, empty_chair opened 2026-08-11T19:09:26 closed 2026-08-12T03:48:38. FOUR are CAPPED - fast_rescue_unavailable, pipe_silent, report_failed, refresh_failed - which is a TERMINAL LADDER STATE, not neglect: LADDER_CAPS passes and its own line reads bounded escalation, a capped alarm stays visible as a standing defect. SO THE LADDER DOES ADVANCE. Incidents close on recovery within minutes - spawn_failed lived six minutes - and others reach capped, which only happens after escalation. My twelve-days-silent claim was really a capped alarm doing exactly what capping is for. WHAT SURVIVES, NARROWED AND STILL WORTH FIXING: run_alert_ladder genuinely has NO caller outside notify.py's own --ladder CLI flag, and nothing schedules that flag. But the ladder advances EVENT-DRIVEN, when a repeat alarm touches an open incident, which is why LADDER_ONE_INCIDENT_ONE_THREAD passes. So what is missing is the TIME-DRIVEN tick: an incident that opens and whose subject never re-fires will not be reminded on the 15, 30, 60, 120, 240 minute schedule. That is a real gap and it is the honest version of this finding - escalation happens only when the problem repeats, never merely because time passed. AND MY BURST WARNING WAS OVERSTATED IN PROPORTION: scheduling the tick would act on ONE open incident, not nine. Triage first is still right, but the risk is one card, not a storm. NARROWED TO ONE FUNCTION 2026-08-12, WITH THE SCHEDULER EXONERATED. Read the failing check rather than guessing at it. tests/test_alert_path_guarantee.py drives n.run_alert_ladder(now=t) in a loop and asserts on gate.edits, the fake gate's record of IN-PLACE THREAD UPDATES. LADDER_ESCALATES_IN_PLACE wants at least 3 edits all into message 777 and gets ZERO. BUT THE SAME LOOP PROVES THE SCHEDULER IS FINE. LADDER_BACKOFF_WIDENS passes with a cadence of 15, 30, 60, 120, 240, 240 minutes, which is only computable because run_alert_ladder ADVANCED next_check_ts on every iteration; and LADDER_CAPS passes because the incident reaches status capped. So run_alert_ladder walks the incident through its whole schedule and terminates it correctly while emitting NOTHING. The defect is in the EMISSION step - _deliver_rung and the _escalation_body / _own_page_body path it calls - not in the ladder's timing. Every one of the twelve ARRIVES_* failures is about an update ARRIVING, which is the same step. THE ONE CAVEAT THAT KEEPS THIS HONEST, and it is exactly the trap I fell into earlier tonight: gate.edits is a FAKE gate's interface. If _deliver_rung emits through a different call than the one the fake records, the 0 is a harness artifact rather than a live defect. That check - does _deliver_rung call what _Gate records - is the FIRST thing to settle, before anyone treats these 16 as production defects. I did not settle it, and after retracting two claims on this row already I am not going to assert a third at the end of a long session. WHAT THE NEXT LANE INHERITS, ALL MEASURED: the backlog is empty and is not the cause; the deadman is red because 16 named checks fail; the file is script-style so run it with python not pytest; the scheduler half is proven healthy by two passing checks; the suspect is _deliver_rung; and the very first question is whether the fake gate observes the real emission call. EMISSION CHAIN MAPPED 2026-08-12, AND IT CONTAINS A BRANCH THAT MAY MAKE ZERO EDITS CORRECT. _deliver_rung at ops/notify.py:2389 edits in place ONLY when msg_id AND _is_anchored(e); _edit_in_place at 2202 calls comms_gate.edit_message; and _is_anchored at 2086 is BACKWARD-COMPATIBLE IN THE FAIL-SAFE DIRECTION - its own docstring says anything that is not a proven fresh send of its own page counts as NOT anchored, SO THE RUNG POSTS, which is the outcome that reaches him. THAT MATTERS BECAUSE IT MEANS 0 EDITS IS NOT AUTOMATICALLY A DEFECT. If the incident is unanchored the ladder is SUPPOSED to post a fresh page instead of editing, and a test asserting at least three EDITS would then be asserting the wrong artifact - exactly one notifying artifact per rung is the stated invariant, either an in-place rewrite plus a bell, or its own page, never both. So the question is not is the emission broken, it is WHICH BRANCH the fixture takes and whether the check asserts the artifact that branch produces. The fixture does set sent with a message id, which points at anchored being true, but I have not confirmed how first_delivery is written in that path. I AM STOPPING THE DIAGNOSIS HERE ON PURPOSE. I have already retracted two claims on this row tonight - nine open incidents when there is one, and the ladder is never run when it advances event-driven - and the remaining question turns on a branch condition in a fixture at the end of a long session. A third wrong assertion in a durable record about the alarm path is worse than an unfinished diagnosis. THE CHAIN IS THE DELIVERABLE, and it is all measured: red comes from 16 named checks, not the backlog; run it with python not pytest; the scheduler is proven healthy by LADDER_BACKOFF_WIDENS and LADDER_CAPS; the emission path is _deliver_rung -> _edit_in_place -> comms_gate.edit_message; the branch is msg_id AND _is_anchored; and _is_anchored deliberately fails toward POSTING rather than editing. Settle which artifact the fixture should expect BEFORE calling any of the 16 a production defect. RESOLVED IN THE PRODUCTION DIRECTION 2026-08-12 - THE EMISSION PATH IS NOT BROKEN, IT BRANCHES, AND BOTH BRANCHES ARE LIVE. RERANKED p2. FIRST, THE HARNESS QUESTION I SAID TO SETTLE IS SETTLED: the fake _Gate in the test DOES implement edit_message(msg_id, body, **kw), records into self.edits and returns True, and _edit_in_place calls exactly comms_gate.edit_message. So the harness OBSERVES the real emission call. Zero edits means the branch was not taken, not that the fake missed it. SECOND, AND THIS IS THE ANSWER: on live state the nine incidents split cleanly by first_delivery. Four carry first_delivery=dedup_satisfied with anchored False - crew_dead, meter_unreadable, publish_stale, spawn_failed - and _is_anchored correctly returns False for them, so their rungs POST THEIR OWN PAGE instead of editing. That is the documented design, not a fault: a dedup-adopted thread is another occurrence's message and rewriting it is the bug the anchor check exists to prevent. The other five carry anchored True and take the edit-in-place path. BOTH BRANCHES ARE REPRESENTED IN PRODUCTION AND BOTH BEHAVE AS DOCUMENTED. SO THE 16 FAILING CHECKS ARE MOST LIKELY A FIXTURE EXPECTATION PROBLEM rather than sixteen production defects: LADDER_ESCALATES_IN_PLACE asserts at least three EDITS, and if its fixture produces an unanchored incident the correct behaviour is to POST, which the check does not count. I am saying MOST LIKELY and not asserting it, because settling it needs the fixture's first_delivery traced and I have already been wrong twice on this row. But the production evidence materially downgrades the sixteen-production-defects reading, which is why this drops to p2. ONE THING WORTH KNOWING EITHER WAY: an unanchored incident posts a NEW page per rung rather than editing one thread, so a deduped alarm escalates more noisily than an anchored one. That is a deliberate trade - reaching him beats tidiness - but it is the reason a dedup-heavy night feels louder, and it is worth a look if he ever says the escalations repeat themselves.

infra.status: ready ||| SWEEP CANDIDATE HELD, NOT RETIRED - re-measured 2026-08-07 by lane-d-sweep-and-echo-generator-fix. The done-detection sweep flagged this gated-but-shipped on shared file citations only. Checked the substance: an untruncated live-line grep of .githooks/pre-commit and post-commit plus every ops/ and scripts/ module finds ZERO callers of ops/scout/closure_gate.py - the only hits are prose about it. The row premise holds exactly as written and the work is still owed. MEASURED 2026-08-12 - THE 100 PERCENT REFUSAL IS A FORMAT MISMATCH, NOT 404 HOLLOW CLOSURES, AND THAT CHANGES WHERE THE GATE BELONGS. RERANKED p2. THE NUMBER, since this row asked whether wiring it would refuse everything: it would. Ran validate_closure over every closed queue row carrying a status - 404 of them - and ALL 404 are BLOCKED, each missing ALL FIVE fields. But missing all five on every single row is not the signature of hollow work, it is the signature of a parser that is not finding fields at all. THE CAUSE: _normalize sends a string to _parse_markdown, which reads LABELLED fields - SYMPTOM:, ROOT CAUSE: and so on. The queue's status field is NARRATIVE PROSE with no labels, so every field parses empty and the gate reports all five missing regardless of how good the closure is. Proved it both ways: a hand-written LABELLED entry passes four of the five fields, while the same content written as prose is blocked on all five. THE GATE WORKS. It is being pointed at the wrong artifact. SO WIRING IT TO ops/upcoming.json WOULD BE A CATEGORY ERROR, and a destructive one - a guard that refuses 100 percent of closures regardless of quality gets switched off within a day, which is the exact lesson ops/dispatch_lane.py records in its own header: an over-eager gate that halts the floor is worse than the prose it replaced. The Director v6 rule this gate implements describes a STRUCTURED CLOSURE ENTRY, and that artifact does not exist in the live flow. That is why it has no caller: not an oversight, a missing counterpart. THE TWO HONEST PATHS: (a) closures start being filed as structured entries the gate can read, which is the rule as written and makes the gate wireable as-is; or (b) teach the gate to read prose, which means judging whether free text CONTAINS a root cause - a regex cannot do that honestly and would produce a gate that passes anything containing the right words, which is worse than no gate. (a) is the real path. A SECOND, SEPARATE FINDING ON THE GATE ITSELF: its GUARD_OBSERVED_RED detector is narrower than its own intent. My labelled test entry described running the sweep before and after with findings falling from about 24 to 10 and accusations to 0 - a real observed red - and the field was still refused as naming no observation. _RED_EVIDENCE_HINT matches mutat, revert, before the fix, fail, red, broke, reproduc, regress, exit 1, rc=1, assertionerror or N failed. A before-and-after COUNT DROP is genuine red evidence and matches none of them. Worth widening before anyone is asked to write to this format, or the first honest author will be refused for phrasing.

modeling.why: Study whether we can measure a coach's on-court impact
modeling.status: MEASURED 2026-08-12T02:1xZ AND THE JOB IS MUCH SMALLER THAN A REBUILD. The ruling is sound and I am not arguing with it: a team-level O/D split failed both prediction targets - margin 10.065 against 9.924 and totals 14.43 against 14.33, worse on both because doubling parameters at these sample sizes costs more in noise than the structure buys - and that genuinely says nothing about the PLAYER question, which is attribution rather than prediction. WHAT THE DATA SAYS: a GENUINE player-level split already exists. Version v5.1 carries 3,394 rows where offence and defence differ, spanning 2003 to 2025 - the widest coverage of any version - alongside v3.6, v4.0, v4.1 and v4.2 which cover 2015 to 2025 with roughly 2,300 rows each. So the descriptive answer the ruling wants is already computed for twenty-three seasons. WHAT IS ACTUALLY MISSING IS 2026: v5.1 stops at 2025, and every version that DOES reach 2026 is one of the fully degenerate ones where offence equals defence equals half the total. So the work is extending an existing genuine split forward one season, not fitting a decomposition from nothing. THIS ALSO SHARPENS AN EARLIER NOTE OF MINE tonight, on the lab-kit row: I recorded v5.1 as MIXED at 6 percent identical. Both readings are the same fact from opposite sides - 225 coincidental ties against 3,394 genuinely split rows - and the useful framing is the second one, because it says the version is a usable source rather than a suspect one.

A rolling mean of our own residuals IS a bias-correction term by construction, so removing bias with it is nearly tautological - the informative part is what it COSTS. Every single unscored game is season_type=2 - ZERO postseason games are unscored - and the count is nearly constant per season at 32, 30, 34, 32, 32, 33, 34. The few days of overlap is exactly what a PER-TEAM warm-up looks like - a team becomes scoreable once she has enough games while others do not. THIS IS THE WALK-FORWARD BURN-IN, a deliberate design property of fitting only on games that finished before, not a gap. SO THE 1615 AND THE 1608 ARE COUNTING DIFFERENT ELIGIBILITY RULES, and a 7-row difference between two population definitions is not a data defect. Before anyone hunts seven games again, the benchmark's own warm-up rule needs stating - that is the reconciliation this row actually needs. THE TOTALS HYPOTHESIS DOES NOT SURVIVE ARITHMETIC. The MARGIN arm scores a game when played[home] >= BURN_IN and played[away] >= BURN_IN - a per-team burn-in, which is exactly the warm-up prefix I measured on the served table. The TOTALS arm then applies a SECOND and STRICTER gate inside that block: if tm.ready(h, a) and Y != 2020. So totals eligibility is margin eligibility MINUS 2020 MINUS the totals model's own independent readiness condition. THAT RESOLVES THE ARITHMETIC THIS ROW COULD NOT. The 123-row difference is not a whole-2020 exclusion, which is why 123 matched neither 147 nor 132 - it is 2020 PLUS tm.ready. This row's hypothesis that the totals basis rests on a different exclusion is CORRECT; what it missed is that there are two exclusions and only one of them is the season. AND THE ENGINE'S OWN HEADER STATES THE BASIS PLAINLY at line 8: n=1615 margin games / 1489 totals games, 2020 excluded from totals. So the benchmark n this row measures against is the engine's own documented population, not an external one. The gap is therefore between the engine as it runs today and the engine as its header describes it - a REPRODUCIBILITY question about our own module, which is a much smaller and better-posed problem than hunting seven games in the warehouse. modeling.name: Worktree isolation is largely illusory: 121 modules hardcode the main repo's absolute path
modeling.header: Worktree isolation is largely illusory: 121 modules hardcode the main repo's absolute path
modeling.status: open - MY OWN PREMISE ON THIS ROW WAS REFUTED BY MEASUREMENT ~20 MINUTES AFTER I FILED IT, and the real finding is bigger, so the row is rewritten rather than closed. WRONG: I claimed a worktree lane would lose the gitignored .env and so falsely report the DB unreachable. Refuted three independent ways. (1) SUPABASE_URL and ODDS_API_KEY are ALREADY IN THE PROCESS ENVIRONMENT, so every child agent inherits them regardless of tree. (2) the scripts do not resolve .env relative to their own __file__ - they hardcode an ABSOLUTE path to the main repo, so they load the main repo's .env even from inside a worktree. (3) EMPIRICALLY: 73 of 296 lane rows declare isolation=worktree, including DB-read modeling lanes (bottom-cs1-coldstart-correctness, top-dal-residual-covariate-hunt, data-triggerready-capture) which all LANDED having done DB work. Isolation has been used 73 times and never stranded a credential. THE REAL FINDING, which is the opposite failure: worktree isolation is LARGELY ILLUSORY. 121 .py files (98 in scripts/ alone) hardcode C:/Users/antho/hardwood-cron, so a script invoked from inside a worktree resolves paths to the MAIN tree and reaches straight out of its own isolation. 19 of those 98 also WRITE a file. So the isolation is PARTIAL AND INCONSISTENT, which is worse than either extreme: the agent's own file edits and its git commit ARE isolated to the worktree, while any output a hardcoded-REPO script writes lands in the MAIN working tree - outside the isolation AND outside the lane's commit. Two 'isolated' lanes running such scripts can still collide, and the record says isolation=worktree on 73 rows, which reads as a guarantee it did not give. Same reads-green-while-wrong shape as everything else tonight, one level up in the infrastructure. PROPERLY SCOPED, NOT OVERCLAIMED: the currently-running damping lane's own script uses REPO only for a sys.path insert, NOT for writes, so THAT lane escapes its worktree for imports only. The 19 writers are the real exposure and are the list to work from - do not assert this of all 121. WORTH FIXING AS: resolve REPO from the module's own location (walk up to the git root) instead of a literal, so a worktree-run script writes inside its own tree. That is a 98-file mechanical change in scripts/ and must NOT be done blind - a script that INTENDS to read the main tree's live state (a builder reading site/ to publish) would break if silently repointed at an empty worktree. Classify the 19 writers by intent first. PREREQUISITE I ALREADY ANSWERED so nobody re-runs it: no past worktree lane produced a false blocked-on-database verdict - the three DB-needing ones landed with real DB work.

data.status: open MEASURED 2026-08-12 AND THE ANSWER IS THAT THERE IS ONLY ONE WOMAN - THE FEARED MERGE IS NOT A MERGE OF TWO IDENTITIES. This row holds back a correct alias on the belief that declaring it would pool two women's records. It would not. Measured on : id 1628922, spelled Azura Stevens WITH the accent, carries 220 games across 2018 to 2025. id 3142010, spelled without it, carries 68 games across 2025 and 2026. FORTY-FOUR GAME IDS APPEAR UNDER BOTH, and on all 44 the game DATE, the TEAM, the POINTS, the REBOUNDS and the ASSISTS agree exactly - same date, same LAS, same box line. Two different women do not play the same 44 games under the same name with the same box score. It is one person recorded twice. A CORRECTION TO MY OWN FIRST CHECK, because it nearly sent me the other way. Comparing min, pts, reb and team_abbr together returned 0 of 44 identical, which reads as two different people. The cause is MINUTES PRECISION ALONE: 1628922 stores 32.4, 34.2, 29.9833 while 3142010 stores 32.0, 34.0, 30.0. Every other column matches on all 44. A precision difference in one column is not a different woman, and an all-columns identity test will say it is. SO THE QUESTION THIS ROW ASKS - WHICH ID IS CORRECT FOR WHICH PLAYER - HAS NO ANSWER, because it is the wrong question. Both ids are hers. The real question is which SOURCE WINS PER COLUMN AND PER ERA, and the data answers it: the accented 1628922 is the fuller and higher-fidelity record, holding 2018 through 2025 with precise minutes; the unaccented 3142010 is the ONLY source for 2026, 24 games that exist nowhere else. Retiring either one outright loses something - retire the unaccented and 2026 disappears, retire the accented and seven seasons and the exact minutes go. THE ACTUAL DEFECT UNDER THIS ROW IS THE 44 DOUBLE-COUNTED 2025 GAMES, which is a live over-count in any consumer that sums across both ids, and is exactly what declaring the alias would have EXPOSED rather than caused. Repair is a merge that keeps 2026 from the unaccented id, prefers the accented id's precise minutes on the 44 overlap, and runs through the append-only path with a pre-image backup. The alias itself is safe to declare once the overlap is resolved. CORRECTION AND NARROWING, SAME DAY - THE CANONICAL PATH ALREADY RESOLVES THIS CORRECTLY. I wrote above that the 44 duplicated games are a live over-count in any consumer summing across both ids. That is true only of consumers on the RAW table, and I should have checked the bridge before saying it. Ran the real GAMELOG_DEDUP_CTE from scripts/gamelog_entity_bridge.py: for 2025 it returns ONE set of 44 rows under 1628922, the ACCENTED id - which is the correct winner, since that is the copy carrying precise minutes. The entity bridge already picks the right id and the right precision without anyone declaring the alias. The raw table still holds 88 rows, 44 under each id, so the duplicate is real in the base data and the bridge is what makes it harmless. SO THE REPAIR THIS ROW NEEDS IS SMALLER THAN A MERGE, AND MAY BE NONE. Nothing needs to be deleted or repointed for the canonical readers; append-only is preserved by leaving both copies and letting the bridge choose. What is worth measuring is COVERAGE: 130 files read and only 8 reference the bridge. That does not mean 122 double-count - most do not aggregate per-player career totals, and a duplicate row matters only where an entity is summed across ids. Naming WHICH of the 122 aggregate per player is the real next measurement, and it is the same shape as the resolve_team call-site split recorded on two-guards-on-one-page-disagree-about-what-a-roster-is: the correct resolver exists, and the open question is which callers reach it. THE ALIAS ITSELF IS SAFE TO DECLARE - it would not pool two women, it would only make explicit what the bridge already infers. Rescoped p2: the identity question is ANSWERED and what remains is bridge-coverage measurement rather than an identity repair.

data.status: ready RE-MEASURED 2026-08-12: HALF FIXED, AND THE HALF THAT IS FIXED ANSWERS THIS ROW'S HARDEST QUESTION. FOR 2026 NOW CARRIES EXACTLY 15 CODES FOR 15 TEAMS - ATL, CHI, CON, DAL, GSV, IND, LAS, LVA, MIN, NYL, PHO, POR, SEA, TOR, WAS - with no minority twin anywhere. This row measured 21. AND NOTE WHICH WAY IT WENT, because this row's central warning was that a naive short-to-long or long-to-short map would be wrong for half the franchises: the repair did NOT follow the majority. This row records GS 282 against GSV 28, so GS was dominant - and the canonical set now uses GSV. Likewise LAS, LVA and NYL over the then-dominant LA, LV and NY, while PHO and WAS won over PHX and WSH. The rule the repair actually followed is THE LEAGUE'S OWN ABBREVIATION, not the row count, which is the right answer and is exactly what a majority-vote map would have got wrong six times. SO THE TARGET VOCABULARY IS NO LONGER A JUDGEMENT CALL - it is demonstrated, in a table, by a finished repair. Anyone fixing the remaining half should adopt the 2026 set verbatim rather than re-deriving it. THE REMAINING HALF IS , STILL AT 21 CODES with six stragglers beside their canonical twins: GS 2420, LA 2200, LV 1760, NY 3080, PHX 2640, WSH 1760. That table has no season column, so the split spans its whole history rather than 2026 alone. IT MATTERS MORE THAN THE GAME LOGS DID: player rating is the impact metric every CEO-facing surface leads with, so any team-level rollup of ratings silently splits six franchises across two codes. MEASUREMENT NOTE for whoever takes it: has NO season column - a WHERE season=2026 aborts the transaction and, in one connection, poisons every query after it. I lost a result to that. MAPPING FULLY VERIFIED 2026-08-12 - THE REPAIR IS NOW UNAMBIGUOUS, AND ONE GOTCHA IS NAMED. Checked every pair by PLAYER OVERLAP rather than by name similarity, because a code map is only safe if the two codes describe the same franchise: LA->LAS, LV->LVA, NY->NYL, PHX->PHO and WSH->WAS each share 100 PERCENT of their stale players with the canonical code. GS->GSV shares 6 of 7. THE SEVENTH RESOLVES CLEANLY: Nadia Fingall appears under GS on 110 ratings rows and never under GSV - but her 2026 GAME LOGS read GSV. So she is a Golden State player the ratings table simply never recorded under the canonical code, and GS->GSV is right for her too. All six pairs are safe. THE REPAIR IS THEREFORE: GS->GSV, LA->LAS, LV->LVA, NY->NYL, PHX->PHO, WSH->WAS on , taking 21 codes to 15, with the target set already demonstrated by 2026. Affected volume is small - 2420, 2200, 1760, 3080, 2640 and 1760 rows. THE GOTCHA, AND IT WOULD HAVE BITTEN: ops/repair_witness.py is the right tool here, but its own header warns that the SELECTION MUST BE STABLE UNDER THE REPAIR - the complement is re-evaluated from the same predicate afterwards, so a WHERE over a column the repair WRITES makes the changed rows migrate out of the selection and the witness cries wolf on a correct repair. The obvious predicate here is team_abbr IN (the six stale codes), and team_abbr is exactly what this repair writes. So the witness must be given a STABLE selection instead - a key or a captured row-id set - or its complement digest will fail on a repair that is right. That is the same trap that fired on the 12087-row note repair earlier this month. I DID NOT RUN IT. This UPDATEs the table behind the impact metric every CEO-facing surface leads with, and the correct witness predicate needs choosing rather than guessing. The mapping is proven; what remains is a careful five-minute repair with a stable selection and a pre-image. I ATTEMPTED THE REPAIR AND IT FAILED SAFELY, WHICH REVEALED THE DEFECT IS TWO PROBLEMS AND NOT ONE. 2026-08-12. The UPDATE aborted on a UNIQUE VIOLATION: the table's is (team_abbr, game_date, player_id, ), so relabelling GS to GSV collides wherever the same player on the same date under the same ALREADY has a canonical row. NO DAMAGE - the whole thing ran inside one transaction, so the pre-image table creation rolled back with it. Verified after: 714485 rows, 21 codes, non-team digest still , zero leftover bak tables. UNCHANGED. THE SPLIT, MEASURED: of 13860 stale rows, 3410 HAVE a canonical twin and 10450 DO NOT. And every one of the 3410 twins carries an IDENTICAL rating - 3410 of 3410, no exceptions. So: (A) 10450 rows are the ONLY record for their key and carry real data under a stale code. Relabelling them is collision-free by construction and is REQUIRED, or that data stays invisible to any canonical-code reader. (B) 3410 rows are EXACT DUPLICATES of a canonical row - same key, same rating. Relabelling them is impossible by the and pointless by the data; they should be retired, and retiring them loses nothing because the twin already holds the identical value. THAT IS WHY A NAIVE RELABEL WAS NEVER GOING TO WORK, and it is a sharper statement of this row's own warning: the trap is not only WHICH DIRECTION to map, it is that a quarter of the rows must not be mapped at all. DO IT AS ONE DELIBERATE CHANGE, not in halves: relabelling only the 10450 would leave the table at 21 codes with the duplicates still holding stale labels, which reads as a half-finished repair to the next person. Sequence: pre-image ALL 13860, retire the 3410 duplicates, relabel the 10450, then prove it with the non-team-column digest over the whole table - that predicate is STABLE because it excludes the mutated column, which is the stable-selection problem I flagged above, solved. THE DIGEST TECHNIQUE IS PROVEN AND CHEAP: md5 over ROW(all columns EXCEPT team_abbr) aggregated over all 714485 rows returns in 5.6 seconds and is what caught that the rollback was clean. RERANKED p2 - DIAGNOSIS COMPLETE, EXECUTION REMAINS, AND NOTHING IS LEFT TO DISCOVER. Everything a repair needs is now measured and on this row: the target vocabulary demonstrated by 2026; the six pairs verified by player overlap with the one GS-only player resolved through her game logs; the 13860 stale rows split into 10450 that MUST be relabelled and 3410 that must NOT be, because they are exact duplicates whose twins carry identical ratings 3410 of 3410; the that makes a naive UPDATE collide; and a proof technique that runs in 5.6 seconds and has already been shown to detect a clean rollback. WHY I AM NOT EXECUTING IT AT THIS SITTING, stated plainly rather than dressed up: it is a multi-step DELETE-then-UPDATE against the table behind the impact metric every CEO-facing surface leads with, the first attempt surprised me with a constraint I had not read, and the proof for a mixed delete-and-update needs designing rather than improvising - the whole-table digest I proved works for a pure UPDATE, but a DELETE changes the row set, so the before-digest must be taken over the rows that will REMAIN. That is a ten-minute design done rested and a way to corrupt an impact table done tired. THE ROW IS NOT BLOCKED AND NEEDS NO DECISION FROM ANYONE - it is ready-to-execute machine work with every input measured. It ranks p2 rather than p1 because the discovery is finished; a lane can pick it up and be done inside an hour with no re-measurement.

data.status: open RE-MEASURED 2026-08-12 AND THE DIAGNOSIS SHARPENS: TWO OF THE THREE ARE NOT PLAYERS KEPT, THEY ARE THE SAME WOMEN SERVED TWICE UNDER TWO NAMES. THE GAP ALSO GREW - 213 served with a live team against 207 in the newest roster snapshot, a difference of SIX, where this row measured 212 against 209. THE ROWS THEMSELVES SHOW THE MECHANISM. On the newest resolve, resolved_at 2026-08-12 03:49:21, serves: alicia florez with bdl_player_id 99338 and in_daily_roster TRUE, AND alicia florez getino with bdl_player_id NULL and in_daily_roster FALSE. megan dileo with bdl_player_id 579 and in_daily_roster TRUE, AND megan gustafson with bdl_player_id NULL and in_daily_roster FALSE. Both women are served CORRECTLY under their current names and AGAIN under their old ones. The old-name rows are the ones with no bdl id, which is exactly why this row observed all three carrying NULL and why an id-based tombstone cannot reach them. SO THE THREE RESOLVE AS: alicia florez getino is a STALE ALIAS of alicia florez, who is on the roster under 99338. megan gustafson is a STALE ALIAS of megan dileo, who is on the roster under 579 - she was renamed, not released, which I confirmed separately tonight. ONLY kayla alexander is a genuine departure: bdl_player_id 337, absent from the feed since 2026-08-03 and last played 2026-07-20. THAT REFRAMES THE FIX. This is not mainly a tombstone problem, it is the CANONICAL-RESOLVER problem in the served table itself - a name-keyed row that the name map already knows is the same person. holds Megan Gustafson and Megan DiLeo against one espn id and one nba id; folding the alias rows into their current-name rows removes two of the six and needs no new judgement, only the map. Only after that fold is the residue a real departure question, and it is one name, not three. NOTE FOR WHOEVER TAKES IT: the table has no computed_at column - the freshness key is resolved_at. I lost a query to that assumption. ROOT CAUSE FOUND 2026-08-12, AND THE FIX IS BOUNDED BECAUSE THE STRUCTURE FOR IT ALREADY EXISTS. THE FOLD IS A PURE LOOKUP - ALREADY links both pairs: Alicia Florez and Alicia Florez Getino both map to nba 5349415 and espn 5349415; Megan Gustafson and Megan DiLeo both map to nba 1629484 and espn 3934218. No judgement is required to know they are the same women. WHY THE TOMBSTONE NEVER RETIRES THE ALIAS. scripts/roster_truth.py builds the snapshot from CURRENT MEMBERSHIP, and its own docstring defines that as bdl-active UNION the 2026 gamelog. The tombstone loop then skips any nkey with `if nk in nkeys: continue # still rostered`. megan gustafson IS in the 2026 gamelog under that spelling - the play-by-play still spells her Gustafson while the box says DiLeo - so she counts as still rostered, is never tombstoned, and keeps her own nkey served forever beside megan dileo. Consumers read DISTINCT ON (nkey), so two nkeys are two players. THAT UNION IS THE STANDING LAW IN MINIATURE: roster membership comes from and NEVER from game history. Defining membership as bdl-active UNION gamelog is game history certifying membership, and it is the same defect as resolve_team's gamelog fallback that killed the gameday chain - a fourth instance of tonight's dominant theme, in the served roster table itself. THE FIX, AND WHY IT IS NOT SIMPLY DROPPING THE UNION: removing the gamelog would drop any player the feed is short on, and the feed already carries 207 against 213 served - dropping her is the failure the missing-history rule exists to prevent. The right change reuses machinery THIS FILE ALREADY HAS: it keeps an alias_of map for PUNCTUATION variants, built by depunctuating nkeys, precisely so an alias orphan is not reported as a departure. EXTEND THAT alias_of TO NAME-MAP ALIASES - resolve each nkey through and treat an nkey whose person already has a current-name row as an alias, not a member. Two of the six extras disappear with no new judgement, and only kayla alexander is left, which is a genuine departure. NOTE: the table has no computed_at column; the freshness key is resolved_at, and consumers take latest-row-per-nkey rather than latest-snapshot. DISCRIMINATOR VERIFIED IN PROCESS 2026-08-12 - THE FIX NEEDS NO NEW DATA AND NO NAME-MAP QUERY. Built a live Membership and read the maps directly. Measured, nkey by nkey: megan gustafson hist_ids [579] in_feed_by_name FALSE person_is_active TRUE; megan dileo hist_ids [579] in_feed_by_name TRUE person_is_active TRUE; alicia florez hist_ids [99338] in_feed_by_name TRUE person_is_active TRUE; alicia florez getino hist_ids [99338] in_feed_by_name FALSE person_is_active TRUE; kayla alexander hist_ids [337] in_feed_by_name FALSE person_is_active FALSE. SO THE TWO CASES SEPARATE ON EXACTLY TWO BOOLEANS: an nkey that is NOT in the feed under its own name but whose PERSON is active is a STALE NAME VARIANT - fold or retire it as an alias, naming the current-name nkey that shares its bdl id.
